title: Morning Edition
dek: Morocco’s election reshuffles parliament amid weak turnout; a super El Niño could sharply raise heat mortality; a global disease study maps where human-altered landscapes concentrate outbreak risk; and Cicero offers a way to act without pretending to certainty.

lead_story.headline: Morocco’s election reshuffled parliament as turnout fell to 38%
lead_story.summary: Provisional results put the palace-aligned Authenticity and Modernity Party (PAM) first with 97 of 395 seats, ahead of the RNI on 66 and Istiqlal on 65. The Islamist PJD rebounded from 13 seats in 2021 to 54, while turnout fell to about 38%.
lead_story.why_it_matters: The vote changes the balance inside Morocco’s elected institutions after a year marked by youth protests, migration pressure and frustration over jobs and public services. It does not displace the monarchy’s broad constitutional power, and coalition formation still lies ahead.

items.headline: A super El Niño could produce hundreds of thousands of excess heat deaths
items.summary: University of Chicago Climate Impact Lab researchers estimate that extreme heat associated with the 2026 El Niño could cause as many as 451,000 excess deaths worldwide from June 2026 through February 2027, with especially large projected burdens in the Sahel and Southeast Asia.
items.why_it_matters: The estimate turns an abstract climate anomaly into a near-term public-health planning problem. It is a modelled projection, not a death count: the useful value is identifying where heat preparedness could matter most, not treating the upper estimate as predetermined.
items.country: Global — especially Africa and Southeast Asia

items.headline: A global study finds emerging-disease risk concentrates where people, livestock and fragmented ecosystems meet
items.summary: A Nature study assembled more than 58,000 outbreak records across 32 diseases and 169 countries. Outbreak risk was often highest in mosaic landscapes where human settlement and livestock overlap with forests and fragmented ecosystems, while the drivers varied substantially by disease.
items.why_it_matters: It argues against a single story in which deforestation or warming alone explains disease emergence. It also shows a major surveillance blind spot: observed outbreaks fall sharply with travel time from healthcare, meaning the global map partly reflects where cases can be detected.

items.headline: India is moving toward restricting junk-food sales around schools
items.summary: India is preparing tighter rules for foods high in fat and sugar sold within 50 metres of schools, extending a public-health push aimed at children’s diets and obesity risk.
items.why_it_matters: School-food regulation shifts nutrition policy from advice to the physical retail environment around children. The consequential question is how the rule is defined and enforced across millions of schools and nearby small retailers.

items.headline: Colombia moved to bar new mining and oil contracts across its Amazon biome
items.summary: An Environment Ministry resolution signed in early August designated roughly 483,000 square kilometres of Colombia’s Amazon biome off-limits to new mining concessions and oil or gas contracts, while allowing existing rights to run to their terms.
items.why_it_matters: The measure covers an area roughly the size of Spain and makes land-use protection a live test of policy durability across a change of government. Because it is a ministerial resolution rather than a statute, its permanence is less certain than its geographic scale suggests.
items.source: The Rio Times / Colombian Environment Ministry context

items.headline: Cicero’s useful middle ground between certainty and indecision
items.summary: Massimo Pigliucci revives the Academic Skeptic idea of probabilia: beliefs can be strong enough to guide action without being treated as certain. The point is not generalized doubt but calibrated confidence that changes when better evidence arrives.
items.why_it_matters: It offers a practical epistemology for decisions made under uncertainty: grade beliefs by scrutiny, separate values from empirical claims, say what would change your mind, argue the other side seriously—and then act anyway.
items.country: United States / ancient Roman intellectual history
items.original_language: English discussing Latin and Greek sources

items.headline: A northern Ugandan secondary school finally has enough new classrooms and toilets to ease daily queues
items.summary: Yumbe Secondary School, with about 1,000 students, opened a new classroom block, desks and sanitation facilities this week. Before the project, reporting found one pit-latrine stance serving 109 boys and another serving 82 girls.
items.why_it_matters: Its significance is deliberately local: ordinary school infrastructure changes how much of a student’s day is spent waiting rather than learning. After recent stops in Guam, Bogotá and Karnataka, the lens moves to northern Uganda and a practical community-scale problem.

worth_your_time.headline: How tightly should you hold a belief?
worth_your_time.summary: Pigliucci’s Cicero essay is worth reading beyond today’s Ideas card because it reconstructs Academic Skepticism as a working method: confidence comes in degrees, scrutiny should scale with stakes, and uncertainty is not an excuse to postpone every decision.
worth_your_time.why_it_matters: It connects ancient epistemology to science, democratic persuasion and personal identity without reducing skepticism to performative doubt.
worth_your_time.country: United States / ancient Roman intellectual history

worth_your_time.headline: A one-tonne Iron Age iron cache reveals trade on a scale archaeologists rarely get to see
worth_your_time.summary: A cache of more than a tonne of iron bars found in northern Austria suggests substantial production and shipment along the Danube around 2,200 years ago—enough metal, Nature notes, for roughly 500 swords.
worth_your_time.why_it_matters: Bulk commodities are often archaeologically invisible compared with finished prestige objects. A surviving shipment gives an unusually direct view of the logistics and industrial scale beneath Iron Age economies.

editorial_review.filler_check: pass — four ranked current stories plus separately researched older-news, Ideas, Human Scale and durable long-read material.
editorial_review.repetition_check: pass — Ethiopia is not repeated after yesterday’s threshold-crossing return. Moldova, HBV editing and EU–Philippines trade are also not repeated.
editorial_review.geographic_check: pass — the current core spans North Africa, global climate/public health, global disease ecology and South Asia; later lanes add Colombia, northern Uganda and the Danube region.
editorial_review.language_check: partial but deliberate — Moroccan local reporting in French/Arabic ecosystems was checked and Human Scale was searched across African, Latin American and Asian local sources; no weaker story was forced to satisfy a language target.
editorial_review.older_news_lane_check: pass — a separate 2–8 week search selected Colombia’s August Amazon extraction restriction because its scale and vulnerability to reversal remain consequential.
editorial_review.ideas_philosophy_lane_check: pass — selected Pigliucci’s reconstruction of Cicero’s probabilia as a dedicated Ideas item and long read, independent of the current-news cycle.
editorial_review.human_scale_check: pass — recent Human Scale geography ran Hama → Guam → Bogotá → Nandagad, Karnataka after earlier Africa/Asia/Latin America/Pacific rotation. Non-U.S. searches were run first across Africa, Latin America and Asia. Today selects Yumbe, northern Uganda: practical school infrastructure from local Ugandan reporting, rotating back to East Africa without exoticism or national-politics framing.
editorial_review.science_evidence_check: pass — the infectious-disease item is a peer-reviewed observational/global modelling study; associations are not presented as proof that any one environmental pressure causes every disease. The El Niño mortality figure is explicitly framed as a modelled projection rather than observed deaths.
editorial_review.contextualization_check: pass — every substantial non-human-scale selection has a URL-keyed reader treatment; Human Scale remains concise.
editorial_review.discovery_check: pass — Morocco’s institutional reshuffle, heat-risk modelling, disease ecology, Indian school-food regulation, Amazon land-use policy, Roman skepticism and Iron Age commodity trade provide distinct frames.
editorial_review.long_read_check: pass — at least one long read is durable philosophy independent of current affairs; archaeology adds a second discovery piece.
editorial_review.local_reporting_check: pass — Morocco lead uses Hespress as actual local reporting, with Reuters and AP as independent external streams. India’s policy story was checked against Indian-policy context; the global science and climate stories are not place-based event reporting in the same sense.
editorial_review.triangulation_check: pass — Morocco uses local Hespress reporting plus Reuters and AP, with provisional results and the monarchy’s continuing role kept distinct. The El Niño projection uses Reuters plus the underlying Climate Impact Lab analysis and independent AP regional climate reporting for context. India uses Reuters with the policy/regulatory context; Nature science is anchored in the peer-reviewed paper and university/research coverage. No modelled estimate is presented as an observed fact.
editorial_review.difference_from_recent: Moves away from Horn-of-Africa conflict and infrastructure emergencies toward an election result, climate-health preparedness, infectious-disease ecology, school-food regulation and epistemology.
notes_for_next_edition: Morocco: return for coalition formation, prime-minister appointment or a material dispute over final results—not routine party reaction.
El Niño: return for observed mortality/food-security data or a major forecast revision, not repeated projections.
Disease ecology: return for independent replication or a concrete surveillance-policy response.
Human Scale: after Uganda prioritize Caribbean, rural Europe outside France, or an island/local-language ecosystem not used recently.
